Copper Quarterly July 2011 # Executive Summary ## Waiting on the mine projects - The LME price fell towards $8,500/t in May, only to shrug off macroeconomic uncertainty and recover to over $9,700/t by mid-July. **Global refined consumption grew q-on-q in Q2** , due to the usual seasonal factors. Production, though, grew by less than half the rate of - consumption, as **mine production was hit by disruptions leaving the market in deficit** . - **We believe the bulk of the deficit in Q2 was realised in China** . However, this was covered by **destocking of the majority of the excess cathode (excluding SRB)** that had been built up over the past few years. This tallies with the declines in SHFE material and the estimated changes in Shanghai bonded metal. - Production growth should pick up and we expect economic growth and consumption to be sustained over the remainder of the year. This will lead to a **balanced market in H2 2011 and a deficit of over 300,000t for the year** as a whole. - We see the price averaging almost $9,600/t in the second half of this year. Delays in mine projects mean that any significant growth will now only occur in 2013 (delayed by a year). As a result, we expect that the **market will be in deficit again in 2012 and the price will rise towards a quarterly average near $10,000/t by Q2** . - The ramp up of **new mine projects will peak in 2013** but will be spread more into 2014 compared to our April report. Consumption growth should be tempered next year due to the high copper prices we forecast, but will rebound in 2013 as the price falls slightly. This will leave the market in a slight deficit in 2013. We forecast refined output will surpass consumption in 2014-15, resulting in small surpluses, leading to the price falling modestly to $9,400/t by 2015. - The price outlook will remain volatile, much as it has been in the first 6 months of the year. However, **consumers cannot currently absorb an ever higher copper price** , so we expect the rise to be capped and any **forays above $10,000/t should be short-lived** . Copper Quarterly July 2011   Executive Summary 

### Focussing on the positive 

Prices plumbed a low of almost $8,500/t in May due to concerns about the effects of the Chinese government’s efforts to rein in inflation and euro sovereign debt on short-term demand prospects and sentiment.  However, prices quickly recovered back above $9,000/t in June and entered Q3 above $9,600/t on the back of renewed investor interest following the latest deal to bail out Greece and a weakening of the US dollar.  The copper price has held above this level in the first half of July, despite an intensification of fears about how the euro and US debt crises will be resolved.  Higher price expectations are largely based upon future Chinese demand prospects. 

The ebb and flow of investor interest drove most of the recent movements in copper prices, but market fundamentals in Q2 provided solid support for $9,000+/t copper on the LME.  While we estimate that the global market was in a significant deficit in the quarter, exchange stocks fell only modestly through to end-June.  This apparent contradiction was due to declines in SHFE and exchange inventory in the US offset somewhat by increases in LME stocks in Asia, and a smaller rise in the LME’s European warehouses.  The growth in LME Asian stocks came from Chinese exports flowing out to take advantage of the arbitrage opportunities between the LME and SHFE. 

SHFE stocks fell as Chinese consumption rose seasonally in the quarter but net imports tumbled to a three year low, leaving exchange inventories to help fill the resulting gap.   We estimate that China recorded a large deficit in the second quarter and accounted for the entire global deficit.  In the world excluding China, the market in Q2 was balanced, as the modest seasonal increase in consumption (following a good Q1) was offset by lower net exports to China. 

In order to fill the gap in Chinese refined supply, total refined copper stocks fell by over 250,000t in Q2, as shown in the table on the following page.  We estimate that this total was made up of declines in off-warrant or unreported stocks (principally at bonded warehouses), as well as draw downs of stocks held in SHFE warehouses.  We expect China to face another quarterly deficit in Q3, as imports are unlikely to rise enough to meet consumption requirements.  This will lead to a further drawdown in the remaining excess off-warrant stocks in the country, taking total 

#### **Major changes since the April 2011 Quarterly report** 

**Demand** : CRU has slightly revised its historical refined consumption numbers for several countries. However, the net effect is small, with consumption in 2010 only 25,000t higher than in our April report. The forecast growth in 2011 is also largely unchanged, but CR

U projects that world refined consumption growth will slow to 2.9% in 2012 as high prices temper growth. We then expect a faster expansion in 2013 taking consumption back to near the level in April. In 2014-15, though, growth averages slightly less than 5% per year, leaving consumption 470,000t lower by 2015 than in our forecast three months ago. **Supply** : Copper mine production for 2011 has been reduced and we now expect a slight y-o-y decline. Our projections for 2011-2015 have also been reduced, as existing operations have lower than expected grades and brownfield projects are leading to maintaining rather than increasing production. Also, projects continue to suffer delays or are not making enough progress. Therefore the peak of new production has been pushed from 2013 to 2014. In a similar way, our forecasts of smelting and refined production have been reduced slightly. **Prices** : Prices in 2011 have been reduced to reflect the lower outturn in Q2 than expected in April and a slightly lower forecast in H2. Further out, a lower rate of production growth leads to lower stock levels in 2013-2014 and prices up by $525/t in 2013 and $550/t in 2014. In 2015, lower consumption and higher production leads to higher stocks and prices up by $130/t. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Quarterly July 2011 Executive Summary 3 non-SRB stock levels to well below 1Mt. As a result, we expect imports to start rising either late in Q3 or early in Q4 2011. The reported stocks-to-consumption ratio tracked by CRU ended Q2 below Q1’s level but on a par with the end of 2010 (see chart below). We now forecast that global production growth at both mines and refineries will be flat this year, but consumption will rise. As we move into 2012, consumption growth is expected to continue to outpace that of production, requiring a drawdown of visible stocks with the stocks-to-consumption ratio forecast to fall to 1.8 weeks by Q4 2012. This provides strong fundamental support to our forecast, with prices rising back towards $10,000/t ($4.50/lb) by Q2 2012. Delays in the ramp up of production from new mine projects will keep the market in deficit and see stocks decline further into 2013. Thereafter, modest surpluses will emerge in 2014 and 2015. As a result, we now expect prices to stay above $9,000/t throughout our five year forecast horizon. The macroeconomic outlook fully supports our view of sustained consumption growth, and along with muted refined supply growth, will lead to a tight market and sustained high prices. CRU’s base case macroeconomic forecast calls for the economic recovery from the 2008-09 financial crisis to continue. Our base case results in global refined consumption growth of 4.3% per year in 201115. This compares to CRU’s forecast for world industrial production (IP) over the period of more than 5% per annum, with China averaging over 11% and the OECD almost 4%. In part we expect copper consumption growth to be slower relative to IP as we have factored in the effect of high copper prices on substitution and downstream inventories. CRU believes that copper prices will start falling from mid-2012, albeit modestly, triggering some end-use restocking activity and easing rationing and substitution trends. However, the lack of cathode stocks to draw upon will mean that until 2013 copper consumption growth will underperform IP (see the chart below). The other major driver of the copper price is the influence of investors. Managed money as reflected in CFTC data has fallen in copper over the past six months. However, the jump in prices in early July back over $9,600/t was accompanied by the fastest rise in the net long position on Comex since 2005. In addition, open interest on the LME rose along with the price, which also indicates the addition of fresh long positions in the market. We believe investor sentiment will remain volatile and this will be reflected in the actual trajectory of copper prices over the next five years. Nevertheless, we expect that on average the support for copper and other commodities from financial players will be maintained over the outlook period for several reasons: - **The “weak dollar”** : Barring another significant financial crisis which causes investors to flee risk, the US dollar is more likely to we

aken against the euro, and other major currencies, than to strengthen. This is due to a combination of the structure of the Fed, the country’s trade and fiscal deficits, as well as a desire on the part of many governments to diversify their currency holdings away from US dollars. This factor will support investor interest in dollar denominated commodities including copper. - **Equities** : The prospects for economic growth in the major economies are rather modest. Thus, aggregate level equity market returns in economies with well-developed financial systems are likely to be rather unremarkable in the near-term and investors are therefore likely to maintain a positive view for copper and other commodities. - **Bonds** : The end of a second round of quantitative easing in the USA and the prospect of rising interest rates around the world will be more favourable to bond investment. This is particularly true in the developed economies, where price inflation is lower and where economic growth is expected to be more moderate. So again, the weight of investor money is unlikely to shift much away from commodities towards bonds. We continue to believe that the resistance of consumers to ever higher prices, both in China and elsewhere, will cap price levels despite the strong underlying support for copper prices from persistent macroeconomic growth, positive fundamentals and sustained investor interest. For example, over the past year higher copper and polymer prices have steadily eroded the operating profitability of the wire & cable (W&C) industry, the largest consumer of copper. This will set an upper limit to the copper price, as there is no incentive for the W&C industry to buy copper if companies cannot make a decent return on the sale of their products. The industry’s use of lower cost competing materials such as aluminium, copper-clad metal and optical fibre stands at a record high. Nevertheless, we expect to see prices trade higher through H1 2012, but to peak below $10,000/t ($4.50/lb) on a quarterly average basis in Q2. After a year of few mine disruptions in 2010, this year is shaping up to be a disrupted one. So far mine production has been affected by extreme and unusual weather in Australia, ASEAN and South America; labour unrest in South America and Indonesia and a technical failure in Papua New Guinea. Lower ore grades and a few technical issues also continue to affect output. As a result, we expect copper mine production to decline by 0.4% y-o-y in 2011. Thereafter, growth will accelerate to 2013 as new projects are brought on stream, before moderating again in 2014 and 2015. Mine production growth of 4.3% per year between 2011 and 2015 is dependent on mine project development, including both greenfield and brownfield extensions and expansions. In all types of projects, South & Central America hosts around 40% of the new potential production. Africa accounts for 18% while Asia and North America hold around 15% each. Only small contributions will come from Australasia and Europe. Therefore, in the next five years new production will come from traditional mining areas, although many of these are facing increasing challenges and higher capex. Refined copper production is forecast to be flat in 2011, with EW production showing little change but electrorefined production up strongly due to the increased use of scrap. Although smelting and refined production i

n Japan has been disrupted by the earthquake and tsunami, this has been largely offset by higher production elsewhere as raw materials have been reallocated in the market.  Investment in new smelting and refining capacity in China should ensure that global capacity is adequate to meet refined copper demand over the next five years.  However, actual production will be limited by raw material availability, of both concentrates and scrap.  Declining concentrate grades will also have the effect of reducing effective smelter capacity at some plants. 

### ...as China continues to lead consumption 

The high price of copper relative to competing materials means that substitution will remain a constant drag on demand growth over the outlook period.  We estimate that consumption growth on a total contained copper basis will be 400-600,000t/y lower than would be the case in an unconstrained world.  Refined intensive, higher value added flat rolled and wire & cable uses will be the least affected and scrap using brass mill products will see the most demand destruction. 

Nevertheless, consumers report good demand prospects for H2 2011, despite substitution pressures and the risky macroeconomic environment.  Chinese growth prospects appear healthy. In particular, we still hold a positive view on Chinese power infrastructure and construction activity.  The State Grid plans to raise investment over the next five years, focusing on the ultra high voltage (UHV) power grid.  While UHV is more aluminium-intensive, we are certain that copper consumption will benefit more from other areas of power grid construction, such as the distribution network.  Rising investment in railways in China should lead to this being one of the

fastest growing end-uses over our outlook period, driven by a 30% increase in the length of the rail network by 2015 including a doubling of more copper-intensive high-speed rail lines. 

The affordable housing programme underperformed against its original targets through H1 2011, but the NDRC announced on 27<sup>th</sup> June that local government investment and corporate bonds issuance will give priority to the construction of affordable housing in the remainder of the year.  We believe that this will lead to accelerating social housing construction in H2 2011. However, there is usually an 8-12 month lag between new house construction and copper usage, so the positive impact on copper consumption will most likely be felt in 2012. 

The home appliance subsidy programme was one of the most effective policies that came out of the RMB4.0T stimulus package China allocated in response to the global economic crisis.  This policy is due to end in November 2011, but we do not believe this will lead to a significant drag on copper demand.  We think that the effectiveness of the programme has been gradually weakening this year, as the number of additional sal

es of home appliances triggered by the subsidy wanes because the number of sales that can be brought forward has declined naturally. We expect that the growth in consumption will outpace that of production in China over the next two years, as the latter faces constraints due to the scarcity of raw materials. This will lead to a rising import requirement in 2012 and 2013. Thereafter, we forecast that the rate of growth in refined consumption will average 7.1%. This is half the rate from the five years to 2010, which is due both to the distorting effects of the exceptionally strong growth in 2009, but also to slower semis market growth as we estimate that the country will achieve semis self-sufficiency in 2013. From 2013 refined production growth should accelerate, leading to the import requirement narrowing in 2014 and 2015. Positive views on consumption are not confined to China. Since April, we have revised up our refined copper consumption estimates for India, with the level in 2010 now 90,000t higher. The change came from a review of our estimates of Indian refined copper exports. We now anticipate that refined consumption in India will grow by 5.6% per annum over the next five years to reach 746,000t in 2015. In addition, the recovery in Japan following the devastating earthquake and tsunami in March is progressing more quickly than we previously expected. As a result we have upgraded our consumption forecast for 2011 to over 1Mt and added a cumulative 120,000t to Japanese consumption over the 2012-2015 period compared to our forecasts three months ago. |Table VI: World

Consumption, macroeconomic factors and the risks due to investor influence have much less skew. A major risk to operating mines is decreasing production from existing operations, mainly due to depletion of high grade reserves and resources. Sources of project risk include knock on effects from major miners having to sequence projects across their portfolios due to a lack of qualified personnel. For smaller companies, tightening funding for new projects also promotes delays. All projects face increasing capex, as the mining industry competes for scarce equipment. Delays may result in higher costs affecting the economics or funding capacity of a project, or late delivery of key equipment delaying the start up of a project. #### Consumption, macroeconomic and investor risks We believe that the balance of risk to other factors that determine the range around our base case price forecast are less skewed than production. Consumption risks are mostly related to the threat of demand destruction from substitution and rationing trends. If this plays out, we would anticipate lower consumption and prices over the period. Substitution of copper

by the greater availability of aluminium wirerod is a key threat to our refined consumption outlook, especially in power cable applications. 

Macroeconomic and investor risks are interrelated, as the 2008 financial crisis clearly demonstrated.  The main short-term issue is that there may be a self-inflicted debt-related policy blunder in either Europe or the USA.  The consequence of unforced policy mistakes in either, or both, would be renewed turmoil in the financial sector, and, depending on the severity of the bungling, descent into recession.  Because of the gravity of these effects we believe that these risks carry heightened but still moderate probabilities compared to three months ago. Nevertheless, how they might affect dollar denominated LME prices would depend on how far a crisis of this sort spread, and the resultant impact it might have on volatility in currency markets.
